passages.t: The death of John the Baptist
passages.happening:
News about Jesus reaches Herod, the ruler of Galilee. He tells his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!” (verse 2). A guilty conscience is speaking.

Then Matthew goes back to tell how John died. Herod had arrested John and put him in prison because of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife. John had kept telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her” (verse 4). Herod wanted to kill John, but he was afraid of the people, because they thought John was a prophet.

At Herod's birthday feast, the daughter of Herodias danced for the guests. Herod was so pleased that he swore an oath to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head on a platter. The king was grieved. But because of his oaths and his guests, he gave the order, and John was beheaded in the prison. His disciples came, took his body and buried it. Then they went and told Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story at greater length (Mark 6:14-29), and the note there gives the history: this is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee from 4 BC to AD 39. Matthew gives him his correct title, “Herod the tetrarch” (verse 1), a ruler of part of a kingdom. In verse 9 he calls him ‘the king’, as people commonly did, though Rome never gave him that title.

Matthew tells the story differently from Mark in one telling way. In Mark, it is Herodias who wants John dead, and Herod protects him because he knows John is a holy man (Mark 6:20). In Matthew, Herod himself wants to kill John, and only fear of the crowds holds him back (verse 5).

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, also tells of John's death (Antiquities 18.116-119). He calls John a good man. He says Herod feared that John's great influence over the people might lead to a rebellion, so he had him killed at Machaerus, a palace fortress east of the Dead Sea. So Josephus gives a political reason, and the Gospels give a personal one: John's rebuke of the marriage. The two do not cancel each other out. A prophet who condemned the ruler's marriage before crowds who loved him was a personal enemy and a public danger at the same time. Matthew's line about Herod fearing the people stands close to what Josephus says.

The names are a known puzzle. Josephus calls Herodias's first husband Herod, a half-brother of Antipas, and says that her daughter, Salome, later married Philip the tetrarch (Antiquities 18.136-137). Matthew and Mark call the first husband Philip. Some scholars think the man bore both names, since Herod the Great gave the name Herod to more than one son. Others think the Gospel writers confused him with Philip the tetrarch. The girl's name, Salome, comes from Josephus. The Gospels do not name her.

A royal birthday feast was a Gentile custom. The Jewish book 2 Maccabees remembers how a foreign king forced Jews to eat pagan sacrifices at the monthly celebration of his birthday (2 Maccabees 6:7). Matthew calls the dancer a ‘girl’, using the same word he used for the daughter of Jairus, whom Jesus raised from death (9:24-25). One girl is given life by Jesus. The other is used to take a prophet's life.
passages.ot:
Jesus had already said of John, “he is the Elijah who was to come” (11:14), and later he will say that Elijah has come, “and they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished” (17:12). The story is Elijah's story again. King Ahab “sold himself to do evil in the sight of the LORD, incited by his wife Jezebel” (1 Kings 21:25), and Jezebel swore to take Elijah's life (1 Kings 19:2). Elijah escaped. This time the prophet does not.

The law John quoted was plain: “You must not have sexual relations with your brother’s wife” (Leviticus 18:16). And a royal birthday that ends in death is old news in Scripture. On Pharaoh's birthday, one servant was restored and the other hanged (Genesis 40:20-22).

Israel also remembered the horror of a rash vow kept. Jephthah promised to sacrifice “whatever comes out the door of my house” (Judges 11:31), and it was his daughter. Herod's oath is another. Matthew's readers had already heard Jesus say, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (5:37).
passages.hard:
Matthew says Herod wanted to kill John (verse 5). Then he says the king was grieved when the girl asked for John's head (verse 9). Does Matthew contradict himself? Some critics think so, and see the grief as a line left over from Mark's version, where Herod protected John. Others answer that a man can want an enemy dead and still be dismayed when it is forced on him in public, at a feast, by a girl's request, with the crowds still loving John. Herod's grief may be for himself as much as for John. He is trapped by his own oath and by what his guests will think.

There is a harder question underneath. Why does God let his prophet die like this, at the whim of a party? Matthew does not explain it. He tells it plainly and moves on. But he shapes it so that John's end points ahead to Jesus' own: a ruler who knows the man is a prophet, a ruler who fears the crowd, and a body laid in a tomb by those who loved him (27:57-60). The forerunner goes first, even in his death.
passages.asks:
Herod kept a foolish promise because breaking it in front of his guests would have cost him face. Ask whether there is a commitment you are keeping only because backing out would embarrass you, and whether keeping it is doing harm.

Notice too what John's disciples did with their grief. They buried their teacher, and then “they went and informed Jesus” (verse 12). If you are carrying a loss, you can take it to him in the same way. Grief is not a lack of faith, and it is wise to let others carry it with you: a friend, a pastor, or a counsellor.

passages.happening:
When Jesus hears about John, he withdraws by boat to a solitary place to be alone. But the crowds hear of it and follow him on foot from the towns. When he steps ashore and sees them, he has compassion on them and heals their sick.

In the evening the disciples come to him. It is late, the place is empty, and they want him to send the crowds away to buy food. Jesus replies, “They do not need to go away.” Then he says, “You give them something to eat” (verse 16). They have only five loaves and two fish. “Bring them here to Me,” he says (verse 18).

He has the people sit down on the grass. He takes the five loaves and the two fish, looks up to heaven and speaks a blessing. He breaks the loaves and gives them to the disciples, and the disciples give them to the people. Everyone eats and is satisfied. The leftover pieces fill twelve baskets. About five thousand men have eaten, “in addition to women and children” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells the same story (Mark 6:30-44), and the note there explains the wilderness, the shepherd and the numbers. Matthew's version is shorter, and it is placed differently. In Mark, Jesus withdraws to rest after the disciples come back from their mission. In Matthew, he withdraws after hearing that John is dead. Grief sends him to a lonely place, and the crowds follow him even there. He does not send them away. He heals them.

Matthew also sets two meals side by side. Herod's feast was held in a palace, for the powerful, and it ended in a death. Jesus' meal is held on the grass, for anyone who came, and it ends with everyone fed and baskets left over. Readers have long noticed the contrast between the two tables.

Only Matthew adds “in addition to women and children.” Counting only the men was an old way to number a crowd. The same words are used of Israel leaving Egypt: “about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children” (Exodus 12:37). The real crowd was much bigger than five thousand.

This is one of the few events in Jesus' life told in all four Gospels (Mark 6, Luke 9 and John 6 tell it too). John adds that the loaves were barley loaves and that a boy had them (John 6:9).
passages.ot:
Bread in the wilderness would remind any Jewish hearer of the manna. “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35). The prophet Elisha once fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, saying, “They will eat and have some left over” (2 Kings 4:43). Jesus feeds thousands with five.

The four actions, taking, blessing, breaking and giving, come back at the Last Supper: “Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples” (26:26). Matthew wants his readers to hear the one meal in the other.
passages.hard:
Did this really happen? Some modern readers have said no. One explanation is that the crowd had food hidden away, and Jesus' example moved them to share it. Another reads the story as a picture built out of the Old Testament, the manna and Elisha's loaves, to say who Jesus is. People who hold that God does not act in the world will look for an explanation of this kind.

The Gospels tell it as something that happened in front of thousands of people, and all four tell it. Christians answer that the Old Testament echoes do not show the story was invented. If the God who fed Israel in the desert was at work in Jesus, it would be natural to tell the event in the language of the desert. In the end, how a reader weighs this story turns on a larger question: whether God acts in the world at all.
passages.asks:
Jesus was grieving when the crowd found him. He still saw them, and he still fed them. Ask whom you are tempted to send away because you are tired or sad.

And notice the order: “Bring them here to Me.” The disciples' food was not enough. It was enough in his hands. Ask what small thing you have been holding back because it seems too little to matter.

passages.t: Walking on the water, and Peter
passages.happening:
Straight away Jesus sends the disciples across the lake by boat while he sends the crowds home. Then he goes up the mountain alone to pray. By night the boat is far from land, battered by the waves, with the wind against it.

In the fourth watch of the night Jesus comes to them, walking on the sea. They are terrified. “It’s a ghost!” they cry. At once he speaks: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid” (verse 27).

Peter answers, “Lord, if it is You,” and then, “command me to come to You on the water” (verse 28). Jesus says, “Come.” Peter climbs out of the boat and walks on the water toward Jesus. But when he sees the strength of the wind, he is afraid. He begins to sink and cries out, “Lord, save me!” (verse 30). Immediately Jesus reaches out his hand and catches him. “You of little faith,” he says, “why did you doubt?” (verse 31). When they climb into the boat, the wind dies down. The men in the boat worship him and say, “Truly You are the Son of God!” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The fourth watch was the last part of the night, from about three to six in the morning. The disciples had been fighting the wind for most of the night. The note on Mark 6 tells more.

Matthew tells this story with three changes from Mark (Mark 6:45-52). He leaves out Mark's strange line that Jesus “intended to pass by them.” He adds Peter's walk on the water, which only Matthew tells. And he changes the ending. In Mark the disciples are astonished, “for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.” In Matthew they worship Jesus and call him the Son of God. It is the first time in Matthew that the disciples together say this.

Peter is often the first to speak in Matthew, and here he is the first to step out. His cry, ‘Lord, save me’, is almost the disciples' cry in the earlier storm, ‘Lord, save us’ (8:25). The word for ‘doubt’ in verse 31 means to waver, to be pulled two ways. Matthew uses it only once more, on the mountain after the resurrection, where the disciples worship Jesus, “but some doubted” (28:17). Doubt and worship sit side by side in Matthew's book.

Christians have long read Peter on the water as a picture of every believer. Augustine, the bishop of Hippo in North Africa, preached that the sea stands for this world and Peter for the church: able to walk only because Christ commands it, sinking when he looks at the wind, and held up by Christ's hand.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, walking on the sea is something God alone does. Job says God “alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8). A psalm says to God, “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters” (Psalm 77:19). Another psalm tells of sailors in a storm who “cried out to the LORD in their trouble,” and then, “He calmed the storm to a whisper” (Psalm 107:28-29).

Jesus' words ‘It is I’ are, in Greek, egō eimi. That is an ordinary way to say ‘It's me’, but it can also be read ‘I am’, the words the Greek Old Testament gives to God himself, “I am He” (Isaiah 43:10). Scholars debate how much to hear in it, as the note on Mark 6 explains. Walking on the sea, many readers hear more than ‘it's me’.

And Peter's rescue sounds like a psalm of David: “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters” (Psalm 18:16). What the psalm says of God, Matthew shows Jesus doing.
passages.hard:
Is ‘You of little faith’ a scolding for being afraid? It needs care. ‘Little faith’ is a word Matthew uses several times (6:30; 8:26; 16:8). It is not the same as no faith. Peter had enough faith to step out of the boat, and enough to cry out to the right person when he sank. Jesus' question names the moment his eyes moved from Jesus to the wind. But notice the order: Jesus catches him first, and speaks second. The hand comes before the word.

‘You of little faith’ is not a rebuke of anyone who lives with anxiety or panic. Jesus said it to someone who had come to him for help, and then he helped him. Anxiety that will not lift is something many believers carry, and getting help for it from a doctor or counsellor is wise, not faithless.

Nor does the story promise that enough faith will keep a believer from sinking, or let him do wonders on demand. Peter walked because Jesus said ‘Come’. The point of the story is not Peter's power but Jesus' hand.
passages.asks:
Peter did what none of the others did. He got out of the boat. Then he looked at the wind and went under. Both are true of most followers of Jesus. Ask where Jesus is asking you to step out, and what ‘wind’ you keep looking at instead of him.

And when you sink, Peter's prayer is short enough to pray anywhere: “Lord, save me!”

passages.happening: They cross over and land at Gennesaret, beside the lake. The men there recognise Jesus and send word all round the area. People bring all their sick to him and beg to touch just the fringe of his cloak. And all who touch him are healed.
passages.hearers:
The ‘fringe’ was the tassel that Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer clothes, as the law commanded. Matthew uses the same word for the tassels some teachers made long to be noticed (23:5). Jesus wore the clothes of a faithful Jew.

Matthew's readers have already heard of a woman who was healed by touching that same fringe (9:20-21). Now a whole region does what she did. Mark tells the same scene (Mark 6:53-56).

Notice where this comes in the chapter. The disciples have just worshipped Jesus as the Son of God. Then he steps ashore and goes straight back to the sick. The one the sea obeys spends the next day with people who can only reach the edge of his cloak.
passages.ot: The law told Israel, “make for themselves tassels for the corners of their garments” (Numbers 15:38), and it gave the reason: “These will serve as tassels for you to look at, so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD” (Numbers 15:39). The people reach for the very part of his clothes that was meant to remind Israel of God's word.
passages.asks: The people of Gennesaret did not understand much about Jesus. They knew he could help, and they brought everyone who was sick. Ask whom you could bring to him today in prayer. Faith sometimes looks like no more than reaching for the edge of his cloak.
